1) Lazily, and never at module level. collector/vendor_client.py is the only place
the endpoint, key and timeout live, and it hands the client out through get_client(),
which constructs vendor.Client the first time something asks for one and reuses it
afterwards. cpu.py, memory.py and disk.py all call get_client() inside collect(), so a
client only ever comes into existence while a job is running. That is not a style
preference, it is the box: metrics-cron-01 has no network route off the machine until
its VPN sidecar has finished coming up, so a client built while a module is being
imported dials into nothing and the import raises before the job has done any work.

2) It spreads to everything scheduled on that host. Every crontab entry on
metrics-cron-01 goes through a single dispatcher that imports all the job modules up
front, so an import-time vendor call does not just kill the metrics collector, it takes
down every job in the crontab. That is what happened the night of the postmortem: one
vendor call at import time and nothing scheduled that night ran, ours or anybody
else's.

3) The route is not there when cron fires. A VPN sidecar is what brings the host's
network up, and it only finishes coming up roughly 90 seconds after boot; before that
the box cannot reach the vendor API at all. So anything that talks to the vendor has to
do it inside a function that runs after that window, and the on-call habit to keep is
never to move client construction or a fetch up to import time, however tidy it looks.
The collector builds its vendor client lazily and shares it. There is one module,
collector/vendor_client.py, that holds the vendor settings and exposes an accessor; the
first call constructs vendor.Client and every later call gets the same one back, and the
three collectors ask for it inside collect() rather than at the top of the file. Nothing
in the service touches the vendor while its modules are loading, and that is deliberate,
because metrics-cron-01 has no route off the box until its VPN sidecar has come up. A
client constructed at import time is a connection attempt made at a moment when there is
no network at all, so the import itself raises and the job dies before it starts.

What makes that expensive rather than merely annoying is how the box runs cron. Every
entry in the crontab goes through one dispatcher that imports all of the job modules up
front, so a module that explodes while it is being imported does not fail alone: it
takes the entire crontab down with it. One vendor call at import time in our collector
cost every scheduled job on that host a night, not just ours, which is why the rule is
stated as a rule and not as a suggestion.

For the new SRE the thing to carry about that host's network is the timing. The route
comes from a VPN sidecar that finishes coming up about 90 seconds after boot, so there
is a window right after the machine starts in which cron can fire a job onto a box with
no connectivity. Code that only dials from inside a function survives that window
because by the time the function runs the sidecar is up; code that dials while it is
being imported does not.
Short version: the client is built on first use inside collect(), never at module
scope, because metrics-cron-01 has no network route until its VPN sidecar comes up, and
an import-time vendor call on that box takes out the whole crontab rather than just our
job.

How the client is built. collector/vendor_client.py owns the vendor settings and builds
the client the first time it is asked for, caching it for the rest of the process. The
cpu, memory and disk collectors call that accessor from inside collect(), which means
one auth handshake per run instead of three, and, more importantly, zero vendor traffic
at import time. Importing any module of the service on a box with no route is a no-op
that cannot fail.

Why. On metrics-cron-01 there is no route off the machine until the VPN sidecar has
finished coming up, so constructing a client (or fetching anything) while a module is
being imported is a network call made with no network: it raises, and the job never gets
as far as its own code.

Blast radius. That host runs every crontab entry through one dispatcher that imports all
the job modules before running any of them. An import-time failure therefore kills every
job in the crontab, not only the one that misbehaved; a single vendor call at import
time in this service took the whole crontab down for a night.

The network itself. The host's route is brought up by a VPN sidecar roughly 90 seconds
after boot. Cron can and does fire inside that window, so treat the first minute and a
half of the box's life as offline and keep every vendor touch inside a function.

1) Three times over, one per collector. Every one of collector/cpu.py,
collector/memory.py and collector/disk.py does `import vendor` at the top, defines its

vendor.Client(...) inside collect() before listing hosts and sampling each one. Since
the SDK's docstring says constructing a Client exchanges the key for a session, that is
three handshakes for one report. Building the client inside the function is the safer of
the two options in general (module-level construction runs at import time, when nothing
is ready and errors are hardest to attribute), but I cannot point at a statement in this
project that says so.

possible: cron runs each entry independently and only the digest is lost; something
supervises the jobs together and a failure could cascade; or the failure is retried and
nobody notices until the data is missing. Without knowing which, the honest answer is
that the visible cost here is a missing nightly rollup and a cron mail.
